items.title: Joe Wilder Part 2 interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 12, 1998
items.q: there were bands like Gus Anheim, Paul Whiteman of course and Duke Ellington was one of my father’s favorites, and there was Cab Calloway and Fletcher Henderson and all these different bands

ctx.x: Do you recall if your parents listened to the music that you liked and how did they feel about it? Did they feel that —

My father, being a musician, is the one that pointed me I guess in the right direction, and my mother too for that matter. But my father used to listen, we had the radio and that’s all you had, and you listened to the old bands, some of which people wonder where I’m coming from with this, but there were bands like Gus Anheim, Paul Whiteman of course and Duke Ellington was one of my father’s favorites, and there was Cab Calloway and Fletcher Henderson and all these different bands, and then we used to listen to…
Yeah. He even liked the syrupy stuff.

items.title: Joe Wilder — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Dizzy joined the band after he and Cab Calloway had an altercation.

ctx.x: Then, after a while, didn’t Dizzy Gillespie join the band?

Dizzy joined the band after he and Cab Calloway had an altercation. He joined the band. He was a joy to be with. A lot of people are not aware, I think, of the tremendous musicianship that Dizzy Gillespie had at that time. Dizzy could sight-read as well as anybody I ever ran into, and in a section he was one of the greatest section players you could want. Whatever you did, phrasing-wise, he did. He lived and breathed whatever you did, as a section player. Many times, he would make suggestions as to how maybe it…
Was he still a cut-up as he was when he played with your dad?
